questions.stem: At common law, a buyer who failed to inspect goods before buying them had little remedy if they turned out to be faulty. This principle of caveat emptor has been most significantly limited by:
options: the Civil Dispute Resolution Act 2011 (Cth) and its statements
the consumer guarantees in the Australian Consumer Law
the Civil Liability Act 2003 (Qld) and its injury scale
the Penalties and Sentences Act 1992 (Qld) and its fines
questions.explanation: Caveat emptor means 'let the buyer beware'. The Australian Consumer Law, in Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), gives consumers guarantees, such as acceptable quality, that cannot be excluded, because consumers usually know less and have less bargaining power than businesses.

questions.stem: Goods displayed on a shop shelf with price tags are generally treated as:
options: an invitation to treat, so the customer makes the offer at the checkout
an offer, which the customer accepts by taking the goods off the shelf
an acceptance of an offer made by the customer when entering the shop
a binding contract that the shop cannot refuse once any customer asks
questions.explanation: Following Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (1953), a display of goods invites customers to make offers. The customer offers to buy at the checkout and the shop accepts, so the shop can still refuse a sale.

questions.stem: In Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893), the company promised to pay 100 pounds to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed. The court held that:
options: an advertisement can never be an offer, because it is not made to a particular person
the advertisement was an offer to the world, accepted by anyone who met its conditions
the advertisement was mere sales talk, so no reasonable person could rely on its promise
Mrs Carlill had to notify the company that she accepted before she used the smoke ball
questions.explanation: The court found a unilateral offer to the world, accepted by performing its conditions, and no notice of acceptance was needed. The company had said it deposited 1,000 pounds with a bank to show its sincerity, so the promise was not mere puffery.

questions.stem: Sam offers to sell his car to Priya for $8,000. Priya replies, 'I'll pay $7,000.' Sam refuses. Priya then says, 'All right, I accept your offer of $8,000.' Which statement is correct?
options: There is no contract yet, because her counter-offer rejected his offer and her reply is a new offer
There is a contract, because Sam's offer stays open until he formally withdraws it
There is a contract, because a counter-offer counts as a conditional form of acceptance
There is no contract, because an offer to sell a car can be accepted only in writing
questions.explanation: As in Hyde v Wrench (1840), a counter-offer rejects the original offer, which then ends. Priya's later 'acceptance' is a fresh offer that Sam is free to accept or reject.

questions.stem: A seller writes to a buyer: 'If I hear nothing from you by Friday, I will take it that you have agreed to buy my horse.' The buyer does not reply. Generally:
options: there is a contract, because the buyer did not reject the offer in time
there is a contract, because the seller set a clear deadline for replies
there is no contract, because a horse cannot be the subject of a sale
there is no contract, because silence cannot amount to acceptance
questions.explanation: As in Felthouse v Bindley (1862), an offeror cannot impose a contract by treating silence as acceptance. Acceptance must be communicated by words or conduct.

questions.stem: Liam offers to sell his bike to Zoe and says she has until Friday to decide. On Wednesday he tells her he has sold it to someone else. On Thursday Zoe says she accepts. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a contract, because Liam promised to keep the offer open until Friday
There is a contract, because an offer can be revoked only in a written notice
There is no contract, because Zoe was required to accept on the same day
There is no contract, because the offer was revoked before she accepted it
questions.explanation: An offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance if the revocation is communicated. A promise to keep an offer open is not binding unless the offeree gives something for it, which creates an option contract.

questions.stem: Two people agree to the sale of a business 'at a price to be agreed later'. The agreement may not be a binding contract because:
options: it lacks capacity, as businesses cannot enter into contracts
it lacks consideration, as no money has been paid over yet
it is illegal, as a price must be set by an independent valuer
it lacks certainty, as an essential term has not been agreed
questions.explanation: A contract requires agreement on its essential terms, and the price is essential to a sale. A promise to pay in the future is valid consideration, so the problem is uncertainty rather than the absence of payment.

questions.stem: For social and domestic agreements, such as a promise between spouses about housekeeping money, the courts generally presume that:
options: the parties intended their agreement to be legally binding
the agreement is void unless it is witnessed by a lawyer
the agreement is binding only if it is written and signed
the parties did not intend to create legal relations
questions.explanation: In Balfour v Balfour (1919), a husband's promise of a monthly allowance was not enforceable because the parties did not intend legal consequences. In commercial agreements the opposite presumption applies, and the parties are presumed to intend to be bound.

questions.stem: In contract law, consideration is:
options: the time an offeree is given to think about an offer before replying
a gift that one party promises to give without asking for anything back
the court's assessment of whether a contract is fair to both parties
something of value given by each party in exchange for the other's promise
questions.explanation: Consideration is the price paid for a promise, such as money, goods, services or a promise to do something in the future. A promise to make a gift is not supported by consideration, so it is generally not enforceable as a contract.

questions.stem: Ben mows his elderly neighbour's lawn for free all summer. Afterwards she promises to pay him $200, but she never pays. Ben cannot enforce the promise because:
options: a promise to pay money is never enforceable unless it is in writing
neighbours are always presumed to intend to create legal relations
his mowing was past consideration, given before the promise was made
$200 is too much for mowing, so the consideration was not adequate
questions.explanation: Consideration must be given in exchange for the promise. Work already done before a promise is made is past consideration and does not support it. Courts do not judge whether consideration is adequate in value.

questions.stem: Ella sells her car, worth about $10,000, to a buyer she met online for $500. Which statement about consideration is correct?
options: The contract is voidable, because the buyer gave consideration that was too small
The contract is illegal, because selling below value is a breach of consumer law
The contract can be valid, because courts do not assess whether consideration is adequate
The contract is void, because the price must be close to the car's market value
questions.explanation: Consideration must be sufficient, meaning it has some value in the eyes of the law, but it need not be adequate. The parties are free to make a bad bargain, provided there is no misrepresentation, duress or unconscionable conduct.

questions.stem: The element of mutuality in a contract means that:
options: both parties agree to the same thing and take on obligations to each other
only one party takes on obligations, while the other receives the benefits
both parties must be of the same age and have the same level of education
each party must pay the same amount of money under the contract
questions.explanation: Mutuality refers to the shared agreement (a meeting of the minds) and the reciprocal obligations that bind both sides. Without it, a promise by one party alone is not a contract.

questions.stem: In Queensland, a person has full capacity to enter into contracts at the age of:
questions.explanation: Queensland's age of majority is 18. Contracts made by minors are generally not binding on them, apart from contracts for necessaries and some beneficial contracts of service, such as employment.

questions.stem: In the law of contract, necessaries are:
options: goods and services suited to a minor's circumstances and actual needs
luxury items that a minor's parents have agreed in writing to pay for
any goods that cost less than $1,000 when they are bought by a minor
goods that a minor buys using money earned in a part-time job
questions.explanation: Necessaries include items such as food, clothing, accommodation and education that suit the minor's station in life and actual needs at the time. Whether something is a necessary depends on the facts, so a luxury item will usually not qualify.

questions.stem: Jack, aged 16, buys a winter school jacket at a fair price and then refuses to pay. Is he bound to pay?
options: No, because only a parent can make a contract to buy clothing
Yes, but only if a parent co-signed the contract with the shop
Yes, because a minor must pay a reasonable price for necessaries
No, because every contract made by a minor is automatically void
questions.explanation: Necessaries are goods and services suited to the minor's circumstances and actual needs, such as clothing, food and education. Queensland's Sale of Goods Act 1896 requires a minor to pay a reasonable price for necessaries sold and delivered.

questions.stem: At 17, Ava signs a contract to buy an expensive gaming console on credit. After turning 18, she confirms in writing that she will keep paying. This is called:
options: rescission of the contract
ratification
repudiation
frustration
questions.explanation: Ratification is confirming, after reaching 18, a contract made as a minor, which makes it binding. Repudiation is a party showing that it will not perform the contract.

questions.stem: In Commercial Bank of Australia v Amadio (1983), the High Court set aside a guarantee signed by elderly parents with limited English. This was because:
options: the parents were legally minors and therefore lacked contractual capacity
the guarantee had not been signed in front of a justice of the peace
the bank's promise to lend money to their son lacked consideration
the bank took unconscionable advantage of their special disadvantage
questions.explanation: The parents did not understand the guarantee and the bank knew of their disadvantage. The court held that enforcing it would be unconscionable. The case shows how equity protects vulnerable people even when they have legal capacity.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a condition from a warranty?
options: Breach of a condition allows termination; breach of a warranty allows damages only
Breach of a warranty allows termination; breach of a condition allows damages only
A condition is always in writing, while a warranty is always agreed orally
A condition binds only the seller, while a warranty binds only the buyer
questions.explanation: A condition is an essential term going to the root of the contract, so its breach allows the innocent party to terminate and claim damages. A warranty is a less important term, and its breach allows a claim for damages but not termination.

questions.stem: A singer hired for a season misses some rehearsals but is ready to perform from opening night. The producer tries to end the contract. Following Bettini v Gye (1876), the court is likely to hold that attending the rehearsals was:
options: a condition, so the producer was entitled to terminate
an exemption clause, so neither party was liable
an illegal term, so the whole contract was void
a warranty, so the producer could claim damages only
questions.explanation: In Bettini v Gye the rehearsal term was not essential to the contract, so breaching it gave a right to damages only. In Poussard v Spiers (1876), by contrast, a singer's absence from the opening performances breached a condition and allowed termination.

questions.stem: In Associated Newspapers Ltd v Bancks (1951), a newspaper printed a cartoonist's work on page three instead of the front page of the comic section, as the contract required. The High Court held that:
options: the front-page term was a warranty, so Bancks could recover damages only
the contract was frustrated, because the paper's layout was out of its control
the contract was void from the start, because the term was too uncertain
the front-page term was a condition, so Bancks could terminate the contract
questions.explanation: The prominent placement of the work was essential to the bargain, so its breach entitled the cartoonist to treat the contract as ended. Whether a term is a condition depends on its importance to the parties when they made the contract.

questions.stem: Raj signs a hire agreement without reading it. It contains a clause excluding the hire company's liability for damage to his belongings. Generally:
options: he is bound only if he later ratifies the clause after reaching the age of 21
he is bound by the clause, because a person who signs a contract is bound by its terms
he is not bound, because a clause binds only if the other party reads it aloud
he is not bound, because exemption clauses can never be included in a contract
questions.explanation: In L'Estrange v Graucob (1934), and in Australia in Toll (FGCT) v Alphapharm (2004), signing a contractual document binds the signer to its terms whether or not they read them, unless there is fraud or misrepresentation. Consumer law may still limit a clause that tries to exclude consumer guarantees.

questions.stem: A couple pay for a hotel room at reception. In the room, a notice on the wall says the hotel is not liable for lost or stolen property. Their belongings are stolen because of the staff's carelessness. Which is most likely?
options: The clause is not part of the contract, because hotels cannot limit liability in any way
The clause is not part of the contract, because they saw it only after the contract was made
The clause is part of the contract, because hotel guests are presumed to read all room notices
The clause is part of the contract, because a written notice is the same as a signature
questions.explanation: In Olley v Marlborough Court Hotel (1949), a notice seen only after the contract was formed at reception was not incorporated. An exemption clause must be brought to a party's attention before or when the contract is made.

questions.stem: A contract to sell goods that both parties know are stolen is:
options: illegal, and therefore void and unenforceable by either party
valid, because both parties freely agreed to all of its terms
voidable, so the buyer can choose whether to enforce it later
a warranty, so the buyer can claim only damages if it fails
questions.explanation: A contract to do something illegal is void, and courts will not help either party enforce it. A voidable contract, in contrast, is valid until the innocent party chooses to rescind it.

questions.stem: A seller falsely tells a buyer that a used car has never been in an accident, and the buyer relies on this. The contract is best described as:
options: voidable, so the buyer may choose to rescind it
void from the start, so it never had any effect
illegal, so the buyer commits an offence by keeping it
valid and unaffected, because of caveat emptor
questions.explanation: A misrepresentation that induces a contract makes it voidable at the choice of the innocent party, who can rescind and may claim damages. The seller's statement may also be misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law.

questions.stem: A contract is discharged by performance when:
options: both parties have fully carried out their obligations
one party has offered to carry out half of its obligations
both parties sign a document saying the contract has ended
an unforeseen event makes the contract impossible to perform
questions.explanation: Performance is the most common way a contract ends: each party does what it promised. Ending a contract by a new agreement is discharge by agreement, and an unforeseen event making performance impossible is frustration.

questions.stem: A gym member and the gym both agree to end a 12-month membership after six months, with no further fees owed. The contract has been terminated by:
options: breach
performance
agreement
frustration
questions.explanation: Parties can agree to end a contract and release each other from future obligations. Frustration requires an unforeseen event beyond the parties' control, and breach involves a party failing to perform.

questions.stem: A hall hired for a concert is destroyed by fire, through no fault of either party, a week before the concert. The contract is:
options: still binding, so the hirer must pay the full hire fee even though there is no hall
discharged by frustration, so both parties are released from future obligations
breached by the owner of the hall, who must pay the hirer's expected profits
void from the start, because the hall turned out not to be fit for its purpose
questions.explanation: As in Taylor v Caldwell (1863), where a music hall burned down, a contract is frustrated when an event beyond the parties' control makes performance impossible or radically different. Neither party is in breach.

questions.stem: Two weeks before a fixed-price kitchen renovation is due to start, the builder emails the owner saying he will not do the job. The owner can:
options: do nothing until the start date, because a breach cannot happen before performance is due
seek specific performance only, because damages cannot be awarded for anticipatory breach
treat the contract as frustrated and recover nothing, because the builder has changed his mind
treat this as repudiation, terminate the contract and sue for damages straight away
questions.explanation: A clear statement that a party will not perform is repudiation, an anticipatory breach. The innocent party may accept it, terminate and claim damages without waiting for the performance date. A change of mind is not an event that frustrates a contract.

questions.stem: Damages for breach of contract mainly aim to:
options: give the innocent party a share of all the profits the party in breach has ever made
put the innocent party in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed
punish the party in breach so that others are deterred from breaking similar contracts
return both parties to the position they were in before they ever discussed a contract
questions.explanation: Contract damages protect the expectation interest, the benefit of the bargain. Punishment is not the aim of contract damages. Returning parties to their pre-contract positions is the effect of rescission, a different remedy.

questions.stem: A carrier delivers a broken mill shaft for repair several days late. The mill owner claims the profits lost while the mill stood idle, but the carrier was never told the mill could not run without the shaft. Under Hadley v Baxendale (1854), the lost profits are likely to be:
options: irrelevant, because a carrier can never be liable for delay in a contract
too remote, because they were not within both parties' reasonable contemplation
recoverable in full, because all losses that follow from a breach are compensated
recoverable, because the carrier should have guessed the mill had no spare shaft
questions.explanation: Damages cover losses that arise naturally from the breach or that both parties reasonably contemplated when contracting. The special loss here depended on facts the carrier was not told, so it was too remote.

questions.stem: A seller refuses to complete the sale of a particular house that the buyer has contracted to buy. The buyer may ask the court for specific performance because:
options: the buyer must prove the seller acted fraudulently first
damages can never be awarded for contracts involving land
land is unique, so damages may not be an adequate remedy
specific performance is the usual remedy for every breach
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable order to carry out the contract. Courts grant it only where damages are inadequate, as is often the case with land or unique goods, because no other property is exactly the same.

questions.stem: Under the Australian Consumer Law, a person who buys goods is a 'consumer' if the goods:
options: cost up to $25,000, the same limit as QCAT's minor civil disputes jurisdiction
cost up to $100,000, or are of a kind ordinarily bought for personal or household use
cost up to $10,000, and are bought only by individuals rather than by companies
are bought from a shop in Australia, whatever their price or the use made of them
questions.explanation: Since 1 July 2021 the ACL's monetary threshold has been $100,000. Goods of a kind ordinarily acquired for personal, domestic or household use are covered whatever their price. Consumers receive the consumer guarantees, which cannot be excluded by contract.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) in consumer contracts?
options: It drafts standard form contracts that every Queensland business is required to use
It enforces the ACL, for example through court action, but does not resolve individual complaints
It decides individual consumers' disputes with traders and orders refunds that are legally binding
It is a court that hears appeals from QCAT decisions on consumer and trader disputes
questions.explanation: The ACCC uses reports to identify widespread problems and can take businesses to court, seeking penalties and other orders. Individual consumers are referred to their state agency, such as Queensland's Office of Fair Trading, or to QCAT or an industry ombudsman.

questions.stem: Sienna's mobile phone provider keeps charging her for a plan she has cancelled and will not fix the problem. Which is the most suitable free next step?
options: A request for the ACCC to order her a refund
A complaint to the Queensland Ombudsman
A complaint to the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman
A claim against the provider in the Federal Court
questions.explanation: The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman resolves complaints about phone and internet providers for free. The Queensland Ombudsman handles complaints about state government agencies, not private companies, and the ACCC does not resolve individual disputes.

questions.stem: A Queensland tenant and landlord disagree about how much of the rental bond should be refunded. What is usually the first formal step to resolve the dispute?
options: Lodging a complaint with the ACCC about the landlord's conduct
Applying to the Federal Circuit and Family Court for an order
The free dispute resolution service of the Residential Tenancies Authority
Filing a claim for the bond in the District Court of Queensland
questions.explanation: For most tenancy disputes, the parties must first try the Residential Tenancies Authority's conciliation service, which also holds bonds. If that fails, either party can apply to QCAT, which hears tenancy matters as minor civil disputes.

questions.stem: Noah buys concert tickets online by ticking a box saying he agrees to the seller's terms and clicking 'Buy now'. Which statement is correct?
options: No contract is formed, because terms on websites are only invitations to treat
A contract is formed only once Noah has attended the concert and used the ticket
A binding contract can be formed, because acceptance can be shown by electronic conduct
No contract is formed, because a contract is valid only if it is signed on paper
questions.explanation: Clicking to accept terms (a clickwrap agreement) can show acceptance. The Electronic Transactions (Queensland) Act 2001 provides that a transaction is not invalid just because it took place electronically. The ACL still protects consumers who buy online.

questions.stem: A full-time employee's written employment contract says she is not entitled to any paid annual leave. This term:
options: makes the whole employment contract void, so she is owed no wages at all
has no effect, because the National Employment Standards cannot be excluded by contract
is binding, because the employee freely signed the contract and received consideration for it
is binding, unless the employee can show the employer acted fraudulently
questions.explanation: The Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) sets minimum entitlements in the National Employment Standards, including four weeks' paid annual leave for full-time employees. A contract cannot provide for less than these minimums, so the term has no effect while the rest of the contract stands.

questions.stem: A clause in a footballer's contract stops him from playing for any other club anywhere in Australia for ten years after he leaves. A court is most likely to find the clause:
options: unenforceable, as a restraint of trade that is wider than reasonably necessary
enforceable, because the player freely agreed to every single term of the contract
enforceable, because sporting contracts are not subject to the general law
a warranty, so the club can claim damages only if the player breaches it
questions.explanation: A restraint of trade is void unless it is reasonable to protect a legitimate interest and not against the public interest. A ten-year, Australia-wide ban is likely to go far beyond what a club needs to protect.
